# The directional capacity law can fail its own centroid Grunbaum bound

This is an exact obstruction to a proposed intermediate scalar argument.
It does not refute OC. The capacity is obtained by minimizing over actual
integer tilts of ambient halfspaces, and its derived one-dimensional
probability law is explicitly identified.

## 1. A genuine three-fiber convex body

Let B be the triangle with vertices (0,0),(sqrt(2),0),(0,sqrt(2)), so
|B|=1. Its barycentric coordinate at the origin is

    ell(x)=1-(x_1+x_2)/sqrt(2).

Set s=sqrt(2)/10 and A=sB. Then a=|A|=s^2=1/50 and A is contained in
B. Let

    C=conv({-1}xA, {0}xB, {1}xA).

C is a compact three-dimensional convex body, and its exact integer
fibers are A,B,A. Its actual mixed area is M=1+2a=26/25.

For a real threshold t define the optimized directional cap volume

    V(t)=inf_(v in R) mu{(z,x):ell(x)+vz>=t}.

These are actual closed ambient halfspaces with nonzero continuous
normal. The affine constant in ell is absorbed into their threshold.
Their middle trace is fixed, and v varies the integer tilt.

## 2. Exact optimization over the integer normal

Let B(t) and A(t) denote the corresponding ordinary cap areas. For
0<=t<=1, simplex homothety gives B(t)=(1-t)^2. It is one for t<=0 and
zero for t>=1. For every real t,

    A(t)=min(a,(1-t)_+^2).

The two endpoints therefore contribute

    K(t)=inf_v [A(t+v)+A(t-v)]
        =min(a,2(1-t)_+^2).                            (1)

Here is a direct proof of the infimum. Put h=1-t. If one term is
saturated at a, the sum is at least a. If neither is saturated, convexity
of x->x_+^2 gives a sum at least 2h_+^2. Thus every v gives at least
the right side of (1). If 2h_+^2<=a, v=0 attains that value. Otherwise
a sufficiently large finite v makes one cap full and the other empty,
attaining a. Closed boundaries have zero planar area and these formulas
remain exact at all thresholds. Consequently

    V(t)=B(t)+K(t),     V(-infinity)=1+a=51/50.        (2)

The initial value is smaller than the original total M because the
optimized integer tilt can discard one endpoint even far down this
one-direction profile.

## 3. Its exact probability law and its centroid

Let E=B intersect {ell>=9/10}. Then |E|=1/100=a/2.
The tail K(t) in (1) is precisely the ell-pushforward tail of twice
Lebesgue measure restricted to E: it is a for t<=9/10 and equals
2(1-t)^2 above that threshold. Therefore the survival function

    V(t)/(1+a)

is the probability tail of the ell-projection of

    [1_B+2 1_E] dx /(1+a).                            (3)

This identification proves existence of the derived law; it is not
being assumed to be the marginal of a log-concave measure.

The B-average of ell is 1/3. The homothetic upper vertex cap E has
ell-average 1-(2/3)(1/10)=14/15. Thus the mean of the law in (3) is

    t_bar=[1/3+(1/50)(14/15)]/(51/50)=88/255.

Since 0<t_bar<9/10, the whole of E lies in its closed upper tail and

    V(t_bar)/(1+a)
       =[(167/255)^2+1/50]/(51/50)
       =291895/663255
       <4/9=gamma_2.                                 (4)

All inequalities are exact. In particular the defect is

    4/9-291895/663255=577/132651>0.

Thus even after minimizing the cap volume over every integer tilt,
the resulting one-dimensional probability law need not have the sharp
continuous gamma_d upper-tail guarantee at its own mean.

## 4. Scope

Equation (4) rules out combining the optimized directional capacity
with an unconditional centroid Grunbaum assertion for its derived law.
Such an assertion is stronger than ordinary probability-tail monotonicity
or the newly proved arithmetic-tail theorem. The density (3) is not
uniform on a convex body and has not been claimed log-concave.

The quantity in (4) is normalized by the directional capacity 1+a,
not by the actual mixed mass M. It is not an OC depth certificate.
The example leaves the original sharp mixed-integer goal unresolved.
